title: Fewest Cells to Join Two Islands
statement:
You get an n × n grid of 1 (land) and 0 (water). Land cells that touch up, down, left or right belong to the same island. The grid has exactly two islands.

You may turn water cells into land. Return the smallest number of cells you must turn so that the two islands become one.

examples.why: The islands are opposite corners. Any path between them through side-touching cells passes 3 water cells, for example (0,1), (0,2), (1,2).
The whole ring is one island and the centre cell is the other. One cell between them is enough. The ring's far corners do not matter.
Diagonal cells do not touch, so these are two islands, joined by flipping either 0.

hints: First, tell the two islands apart. A flood fill from any land cell marks one whole island.
Then the question is: how far is the nearest cell of the other island? Searching from one starting cell at a time repeats a lot of work.

Put every cell of the first island in a BFS queue at distance 0 and expand all of them together, one ring of water at a time. The first time you step onto land that is not marked, the current ring number is the answer.

explain.intuition:
Two steps. First find one island completely: flood fill (DFS) from the first land cell you see, and mark every cell you reach. Everything else that is land is the second island.

Now grow the first island outward one layer at a time. That is a BFS that starts from all its cells at once (multi-source BFS). After one round you have every water cell at distance 1, after two rounds distance 2, and so on. The first time the frontier touches a land cell that is not marked, you have crossed the gap. The number of water layers you went through is the number of cells to flip. Starting the BFS from the whole island is what makes it O(n²) instead of a separate search from every cell.
steps: Find any land cell. Flood fill from it, marking each cell (for example set it to 2) and pushing it into the BFS queue.
Set steps = 0. Process the queue level by level.
For each cell in the current level, look at its four neighbours. If a neighbour is 1, the other island is reached: return steps.
If a neighbour is 0, mark it as visited (2) and add it to the next level.
pitfalls: Counting diagonal neighbours. Islands and paths use only up, down, left and right.
Running BFS from a single cell of the first island. The closest point of the island may be elsewhere, as the ring example shows.
Returning steps + 1 or counting the land cells. The answer is the number of water cells crossed, which is the level at which land is found.

solutions.title: Closest pair of cells
solutions.idea: Mark the first island with a flood fill. The answer is the smallest Manhattan distance between a cell of one island and a cell of the other, minus 1: a shortest path between the closest pair crosses only water.

solutions.title: Flood fill, then multi-source BFS
solutions.idea: Mark the first island and seed a BFS with all of its cells. Expand through water one layer at a time; the layer that first touches unmarked land is the answer.

followups: There are k islands and you want to join all of them with as few flipped cells as possible. Why does this become much harder?
Return the actual cells to flip, not just how many. What would you store during the BFS?
